title: This Is For You
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder writes to exhausted founders who are excellent at building but drowning in the business itself. She validates the impossible feeling of daily urgency, fires, and unmet lists, then diagnoses the root cause: not team inadequacy but a clarity gap between responsibility (doing work) and ownership (protecting outcomes with authority). Founders typically install systems and hire people but continue to feel essential because real ownership—with decision-making power—has never been clearly defined. Mulder's framework is elegantly simple: identify the one constraint whose removal would make everything else easier, then go all in on fixing that before pursuing the next system or hire. The breakthrough isn't operational but philosophical, requiring founders to stop moving long enough to see the pattern and distinguish between what needs their personal involvement and what needs clarity instead. She describes the specific work inside portfolio companies: mapping the gap between assigned responsibility and actual authority, documenting ownership definitions in writing, and stepping back far enough to let it work. Her message is that good founders already have good teams; the problem is architecture, not talent, and the fix lies in clarity, not more optimization.
points: Founder burnout stems from apparent team inadequacy but typically reflects a clarity gap between responsibility (task execution) and ownership (protecting outcomes with authority).
The leverage question shifts from managing seventeen competing priorities to identifying the single constraint whose removal enables everything else to flow: finding the one thing.
Founders feel they must stay involved in decisions to maintain quality, but paradoxically their involvement prevents delegation by failing to grant real authority alongside responsibility.
Clarity in writing about what ownership means in the company is the prerequisite for delegation to work; without it, the founder becomes inevitable.
Exhaustion combined with demonstrated competence is not a contradiction but a signal of misaligned accountability architecture.
quotes: You're good at this. And you're exhausted. And those two things live at the same time. You wake up already behind. There are decisions waiting for you before you've had coffee.
The thing that changed everything wasn't a new system. It was a different question. What's the one thing, right now, in this season, that if fixed would make everything else easier?
It looks like a team problem. Like people who aren't stepping up or aren't capable or aren't doing enough. But most of the time it's a clarity problem.

The team doesn't know what owning something actually means here. They know their tasks. They know their responsibilities. But nobody has ever made it clear, specifically, in writing, with real authority attached, what it means to fully own an outcome in this company.

Finding that gap between what someone is responsible for and what they actually own. Installing the clarity that lets people move without waiting.” Archived from Summer Mulder Substack on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
